name: Paul
bio: Saul, a young man, was present at Stephen's stoning, where the witnesses laid their garments at his feet (Acts 7:58). His conversion and transformation into the apostle Paul are told in detail in the chapters ahead. Saul approved of Stephen's death and, in the great persecution that followed, ravaged the church, entering homes and dragging off men and women to prison (Acts 8:1-3). Still breathing threats against the church, Saul obtained letters authorizing him to arrest believers in Damascus, but on the road a blinding light from heaven knocked him to the ground, and he heard Jesus's voice asking why he persecuted him. Blind for three days, Saul was found by Ananias, whom the Lord had sent despite his fears, since Saul was a chosen instrument to carry Jesus's name to the Gentiles; Ananias restored his sight, and Saul was baptized and filled with the Holy Spirit. He immediately began preaching Christ in the Damascus synagogues to the astonishment of those who had known him as a persecutor, until a Jewish plot to kill him forced the disciples to lower him from the city wall in a basket. In Jerusalem, the disciples were afraid of him until Barnabas vouched for him before the apostles, after which Saul preached boldly until another plot forced him to flee to Tarsus (Acts 9:1-30). Barnabas found Saul in Tarsus and brought him to Antioch, where they taught together for a year among the growing number of Gentile believers, who were first called Christians there; when the prophet Agabus foretold a famine, Saul and Barnabas were entrusted with carrying relief to the believers in Judea (Acts 11:25-30). At Paphos on Cyprus, when the sorcerer Bar-jesus (Elymas) tried to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus from the faith, Saul, filled with the Holy Spirit, denounced him and declared he would be struck blind, which happened at once; from this point the narrative calls him by his Roman name, Paul. In Antioch of Pisidia, Paul preached in the synagogue a lengthy sermon tracing Israel's history to David and then to Jesus as the promised Savior, raised from the dead and offering forgiveness of sins; when the Jews responded with envy and contradiction the following sabbath, Paul and Barnabas declared they would turn to the Gentiles, as the Lord had commanded, and many believed, though persecution drove them out to Iconium (Acts 13:1-52). At Lystra, Paul healed a man crippled from birth who had never walked; the crowds hailed him as the god Mercurius and Barnabas as Jupiter, moving to sacrifice to them, which Paul and Barnabas protested and barely restrained. Jews from Antioch and Iconium then stirred the crowd to stone Paul and drag him out of the city for dead, but he rose and continued on, preaching through Derbe and back through Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, appointing elders, before returning to report to the church at Antioch in Syria (Acts 14:1-28). When believers from Judea insisted that Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved, Paul and Barnabas took the dispute to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, reporting the miracles God had worked among the Gentiles through them; the council sided with Peter and James, requiring only a few basic restrictions, and sent Paul and Barnabas back to Antioch with the decision in writing (Acts 15:1-35). Some time later, Barnabas wanted to take John Mark on a return visit to the churches, but Paul refused, since Mark had deserted them in Pamphylia; the disagreement grew so sharp that the two separated, and Paul took Silas as his new companion, departing through Syria and Cilicia (Acts 15:36-41). In Lystra, Paul took on the disciple Timothy as a traveling companion, having him circumcised because of the Jews in the region. Forbidden by the Spirit from preaching in Asia, Paul saw a vision of a man of Macedonia begging for help and so crossed over to Philippi, where he and his companions won Lydia and her household to faith. When Paul cast an unclean spirit of divination out of a slave girl whose masters had profited from her fortune-telling, her enraged owners had Paul and Silas seized, beaten, and thrown into prison. At midnight, as Paul and Silas prayed and sang, an earthquake shook open the prison doors; Paul stopped the jailer from killing himself, and the jailer and his household believed and were baptized. The next day, after the magistrates learned the two were Roman citizens, Paul insisted they be released openly rather than secretly, and they left for Lydia's house before departing the city (Acts 16:1-40).  In Thessalonica, Paul reasoned from the scriptures that Christ had to suffer and rise again, persuading some Jews and many Greeks, but unbelieving Jews stirred up a mob and attacked Jason's house looking for him; Paul and Silas were sent away by night to Berea, where the Jews searched the scriptures eagerly and many believed, until Thessalonian agitators followed and stirred up trouble there too, forcing Paul on to Athens while Silas and Timothy stayed behind. In Athens, troubled by the city's idolatry, Paul reasoned in the synagogue and marketplace and was brought before the Areopagus, where he preached about the "unknown god" worshiped in ignorance, declaring that God made the world, gives life to all, and has appointed a day of judgment through the man he raised from the dead; some mocked at the mention of resurrection, but others wanted to hear more, and a few believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris (Acts 17:1-34). In Corinth, Paul stayed and worked with the tentmakers Aquila and Priscilla, reasoning in the synagogue each sabbath; when Silas and Timothy arrived, he testified boldly that Jesus was the Christ, but after the Jews opposed and blasphemed him, he turned to the Gentiles and moved to the house of Justus next to the synagogue. Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believed along with many other Corinthians, and the Lord assured Paul in a vision that no one would harm him there; he stayed a year and six months teaching. When the Jews brought him before the proconsul Gallio, the charge was dismissed before Paul could even speak in his defense. He eventually sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, stopping in Ephesus, then Caesarea and Antioch, before traveling through Galatia and Phrygia strengthening the disciples (Acts 18:1-23).  At Ephesus, Paul found disciples who had received only John's baptism and knew nothing of the Holy Spirit; after he explained the baptism of Jesus, they were baptized and received the Holy Spirit, speaking in tongues and prophesying when he laid hands on them. He taught boldly in the synagogue and then in the school of Tyrannus for two years, and God worked such miracles through him that even cloths that had touched him healed the sick; when seven sons of the Jewish priest Sceva tried to exorcise a spirit in Jesus's name as Paul did, the spirit overpowered them instead, spreading fear and magnifying the Lord's name throughout the city. Paul sent Timothy and Erastus ahead into Macedonia while he stayed in Asia. When the silversmith Demetrius stirred up a riot over the threat Paul's preaching posed to the worship of Diana, the mob seized Paul's companions Gaius and Aristarchus and filled the theater in confusion for about two hours before the town clerk calmed them and dismissed the assembly (Acts 19:1-41).  After the Ephesian riot, Paul traveled through Macedonia and Greece, then set out for Jerusalem with companions including Sopater, Aristarchus, Secundus, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, Tychicus, and Trophimus. At Troas, when the young man Eutychus fell asleep and dropped dead from a third-story window during Paul's long sermon, Paul embraced him and restored him to life before continuing to preach until daybreak. Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul bypassed Ephesus but summoned its elders to Miletus, where he reminded them of his tearful, selfless ministry among them, warned that he would see them no more and that false teachers would arise to prey on the flock, and commended them to God's grace; the elders wept and embraced him before he sailed on (Acts 20:1-38).  Sailing on toward Jerusalem, Paul and his companions were warned by disciples at Tyre and by the prophet Agabus at Caesarea, who bound his own hands and feet to foretell that Paul would be bound and handed to the Gentiles; Paul insisted he was ready even to die for the Lord's name, and the believers reluctantly let him go. In Jerusalem, Paul reported his ministry to James and the elders, who asked him to join four men under a vow and pay for their purification to quiet rumors that he taught against the law; Paul agreed and entered the temple with them. But Jews from Asia saw him there, stirred up a mob by falsely claiming he had brought the Gentile Trophimus into the temple, and dragged him out to beat him to death, until the Roman commander and soldiers intervened and arrested him, carrying him off amid the crowd's violence. On the stairs of the barracks, Paul asked and received permission to address the people, speaking to them in Hebrew (Acts 21:1-40).  Given leave to address the crowd from the stairs, Paul spoke in Hebrew, recounting his strict upbringing under Gamaliel, his earlier persecution of the church, his blinding vision of Jesus on the Damascus road, and Ananias restoring his sight and commissioning him; he added that in a later temple vision the Lord had told him to leave Jerusalem because the Jews would reject his testimony and sent him instead to the Gentiles. At the mention of the Gentiles the crowd erupted, demanding his death, and the commander had him bound for scourging until Paul revealed he was a Roman citizen by birth, which halted the examination and alarmed the commander for having bound him. The next day, the commander released him and summoned the chief priests and council to hear the charges against him (Acts 22:1-30).
